messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Kwame is a 68-year-old widowed African American policy analyst who came to treatment after months of telling himself that surviving should have been enough. The illness that changed his life began abruptly. He had been at work, reading through a dense policy brief and preparing notes for a meeting, when he was hit by a sudden wave of physical collapse that did not feel explainable or manageable. What remained most vivid was not a medical summary but the immediate conviction that his body had turned against him without warning. In the hospital, surrounded by alarms, urgent voices, and the sight of clinicians moving quickly around him, he believed he might die. He remembers moments of watching people speak over him and around him while his attention narrowed to his own breathing and the frightening sense that he could no longer rely on his body to do what it had always done automatically. For Kwame, the terror was not abstract. It was the realization, in real time, that the threat was inside him.

In the weeks after he was discharged, he expected to feel shaken and then gradually relieved. Instead, the experience seemed to remain unfinished. At times he could describe what happened in a flat, detached way, almost as if he were reporting on another man’s hospitalization. He would recount the sequence of events to his adult daughter or to his physician with a strange numbness that unsettled him; he noticed that he sounded calm while feeling cut off, as though the memory belonged to a stranger. At other times the opposite happened. A bodily sensation, a pause in his breathing, or the effort of trying to remember a detail from the hospital would bring the whole experience forward with crushing immediacy. Then the illness no longer felt like something in the past. It felt current, as if he were once again inside that hospital bed with danger unfolding around him. When that happened he became so emotionally overwhelmed that he had to stop talking, sit down, and wait for the surge to pass.

As the months went on, Kwame became increasingly preoccupied with the idea that his body was fundamentally unreliable. He had come to believe that he could no longer trust it, not even in ordinary moments. If his heart rate shifted, if he felt tired, if his stomach tightened, he did not take these as passing sensations. To him they were warnings that another crisis could begin at any moment. What frightened him most was that his body continued to react as though danger were still present even when he knew, rationally, that he was sitting safely in his own living room. This left him feeling betrayed by himself. He said more than once that his body was acting like an enemy, and that no amount of reassurance fully reached the place in him that expected catastrophe.

That expectation shaped his daily life. At home, where he used to enjoy quiet evenings reading or reviewing reports, he found himself unable to settle. He stayed alert to every internal shift, every change in tension, every sign that something might be wrong. Even in his own house he felt on guard. He noticed that he sat upright, shoulders tight, listening to his body rather than relaxing into the room. Sleep and rest no longer felt restorative because his system never seemed to stand down. He was distressed by how tense he felt all the time, as though he were poised for bad news.

The effects showed up at work as well. Kwame had spent decades in policy analysis and took pride in his precision, but now concentration came in fragments. During meetings he would lose the thread of discussion and find himself pulled inward by a sensation in his chest or by the return of the hospital memory. While trying to read long documents, he would discover that he had scanned the same paragraph repeatedly without absorbing it. This was humiliating to him. He had always seen himself as measured, intellectually steady, and dependable. Now he worried that colleagues might notice the lapses, though he said little about them. His world became smaller and more effortful, organized around managing the possibility of danger in his own body.

Alongside this was a more private despair. Kwame had begun to think that he would never feel normal emotions again. Since the illness, his inner life seemed split between numbness and overpowering fear, with little room for ease, pleasure, or the ordinary warmth he remembered from before. As a widower, he had already learned to live with loss; this felt different, as though something basic in him had gone missing. He sought help only after recognizing that the pattern was not loosening with time. What finally brought him in was not one dramatic incident but the accumulation of living in a constant state of internal watchfulness, struggling to think clearly, and feeling estranged from himself. He said he wanted to know whether it was possible to live in his body again without feeling hunted by it, and he was deeply afraid that the answer might be no.
